extracted.intended_audience: Navy program managers, NPRDC staff, analysts performing OMB A-76 cost comparisons for MIS/HRM systems
extracted.subtask_short: in-house vs contract MIS cost comparison
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating whether a Management Information System (HRMIN) should remain in‑house or be contracted out, using OMB Circular A‑76 cost-comparison methodology and site/ vendor evaluation criteria. Includes benchmarking vendor offers, enumerating cost elements, and weighing system performance, security, control, support, and costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: System Performance and Reliability
rubrics_metrics.description: System performance was defined as how well the system supports and performs the function of the application running on it. System reliability was defined as the ability of a system to provide dependable support on a continuous basis (90% up-time and a back-up system).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed as the #1 evaluation criterion by the Program Manager and users in the Booz‑Allen and Hamilton study; used to compare alternative locations (NPRDC, NPS, timesharing). High performance/reliability implies ability to support application functions and meet uptime/back-up expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: System and Data Security
rubrics_metrics.description: Security was defined as providing an acceptable level of protection against unauthorized access to the system and to HRM Survey data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluates the alternative's ability to prevent unauthorized access to system/software/data. Considerations include vendor/client safeguards, access procedures, and protections against 'unauthorized trespassing on others' property' in timesharing environments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Management Control
rubrics_metrics.description: The key management control factor for any alternative is the ease with which the sponsor can monitor the performance of the system and, if necessary, re-direct the management or content of the application so that the plans or objectives for the system are effectively used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assesses how readily the sponsor can oversee and influence operation/content. Important for ensuring system objectives are met and for making operational redirections when needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintenance and Operational Support
rubrics_metrics.description: The ability of the managing organization at the location to provide adequate personnel resources for the maintenance and operation of the system hardware and software.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Considers availability and qualifications of System Manager, Analyst/Programmer, operators, and other support staff; examines whether software was written in-house (reduces conversion/maintenance issues) and whether the site can provide ongoing logistics/support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost
rubrics_metrics.description: Cost was the final criterion used to evaluate the alternative locations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Figure legend: '**A HIGH RATING FOR THIS CATEGORY MEANS LOWER COSTS; HIGH IS COST‑BENEFICIAL.' The text notes cost is often the least important criterion to users, but large cost differences can dominate recommendations (e.g., timesharing found five times higher cost vs in‑house in a referenced study).

rubrics_metrics.name: Benchmarking (vendor evaluation method)
rubrics_metrics.description: Benchmarking is the method of evaluating potential vendors during competitive procurement. A benchmark is a mix of requirements representative of the user's projected workload over the life of the system; mandatory and desired specifications (e.g., data storage, software requirements) are presented in the RFP. Programs to test specific user requirements are part of the benchmark; potential clients run the benchmark job and are graded using a scheme devised by the proposer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to elicit vendor capability and price for a representative workload. Vendors are scored on benchmark performance and compliance with mandatory/desired specs; benchmarking results feed into cost and capability comparisons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vendor charge factors for timesharing/computer services
rubrics_metrics.description: Vendors base charges for their services on all or a combination of: (1) Connect time to the computer—the duration of an active transmission link; (2) CPU time [Processing]—the period a program occupies the CPU; (3) Storage capacity—required for the user's programs or data files; (4) Channel time — duration of channel use (sometimes measured by I/O requests); (5) Additional charges—may be made for file access, languages, applications programs, and terminal/communication equipment rentals. [Ex: SPSS royalty fees] (Hagin and Mader, 1979, p.316).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When comparing vendor quotes, adjust and benchmark vendor price schedules (e.g., TSP Authorized Schedule) and consider which charge factors apply to the user's profile; competitive bidding and negotiation tactics can greatly affect final costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost elements for in-house service organizations
rubrics_metrics.description: A cost element is a basic unit of cost such as labor or materials. Major cost elements associated with a service organization include: 1. Direct Labor; 2. Fringe Benefits on Labor; 3. Operations Overhead; 4. Other Direct Costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accumulate all relevant cost elements per OMB Circular A‑76 framework to compute total in‑house cost. These form the basis of the cost comparison against vendor/contract alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Realized Value model (Potential, Received, Utilization)
rubrics_metrics.description: Benefit assessment postulates three benefit factors: Potential Contribution (P) — value attached on basis of predetermined specifications; Received Value (R) — portion of potential normally received by users; Utilization Value (U) — portion of received value users can actually apply. Realized Value = Potential Contribution x Received Value x Utilization (a scale x scale x percent x percent). (Navy Personnel Research and Development Center, 1974, p.10).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This multiplicative model measures perceived effectiveness/value of information systems and emphasizes that potential capability only yields value if delivered and actually utilized by users. Useful when quantifying intangible benefits in cost‑benefit discussions.

rubrics_metrics.name: MIS benefits / time‑compression criteria (Krauss list)
rubrics_metrics.description: An MIS may help: 1) Render faster decisions (detect/authenticate opportunity; identify/isolate problems; define/analyze situations; evaluate/appraise alternatives); 2) Accomplish more in available time (think more deeply, ponder other variables, gauge ramifications, investigate more alternatives); 3) Make a more thorough analysis (review more meaningful information, obtain better collection of viewpoints, use advanced techniques, simulate conditions, ask more 'what if' questions). The central point is time—the time made available by computer processing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are the expected benefits used to argue for MIS development; when evaluating alternatives, consider how each option enables faster decisionmaking, deeper analysis, and greater throughput via time compression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Management control cycle / real‑time management control
rubrics_metrics.description: A system of controls aims to minimize time between the point at which a condition goes out of control and the point at which a correction is successfully executed. Stages include measurement/detection, communication, situation analysis, decisionmaking, communication of responsibilities, setup, and execution. Real‑time MISs can compress these intervals in measurement, detection, communication, situation analysis, decisionmaking, and corrective action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate alternatives by their capacity to shorten the management control (react & rectify) cycle; shorter cycles permit substantial economy and higher quality decisions—particularly important for time‑sensitive 'people problems' in HRM.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typical disadvantages of timesharing/commercial services
rubrics_metrics.description: Listed disadvantages (Hagin and Mader, 1974, p.315-316): 1) Timesharing is needlessly expensive for users who do not benefit from quick responses or have high transaction volumes; limited terminal speeds can increase communications charges; remote batch processing increases turnaround to minutes/hours. 2) Introduces considerable overhead that users ultimately pay for (costly OS, communications costs, vendor marketing/admin/taxes/profit). 3) Usage can be delayed minutes to hours due to telephone line or computer difficulties; technical problems. 4) Data security problems are accentuated; safeguarding programs/data and vendor access procedures are required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When considering timesharing as an alternative, weigh these operational, cost, delay, and security drawbacks against benefits and vendor mitigations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typical benefits of contracting / computer service bureaus
rubrics_metrics.description: Example benefits listed for contracting to a computer service organization include: 1) Fewer programming errors; 2) No training required; 3) Known costs; 4) No equipment maintenance (and other logistic support); 5) Minimum personnel problems; 6) Increased experience and capability for future expanded efforts; 7) Greater capability for handling varying workload.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These benefits are the outputs expected for costs incurred and should be listed and weighed against in‑house benefits/costs in the A‑76 cost comparison.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria ordering and stakeholder weighting
rubrics_metrics.description: The criteria and their order of importance were established by the Program Manager and the users of HRMIN; Figure 6 displays criteria in descending order of importance to the Navy personnel interviewed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When performing evaluations, apply stakeholder-defined weightings/ordering (system performance/reliability first, then security, management control, maintenance/support, cost) rather than treating all criteria equally.
